# Tobit Chapter 14 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Summary
Chapter 14 is the concluding chapter of Tobit — Tobit's deathbed prophecy, death, and Tobias's long life culminating in witnessing Nineveh's fall. 14 divergences were logged across the 15 verses, many concentrated in the prophetic speech (vv. 3–11) and the final genealogical summary (vv. 12–15).

---

## Disagreement Table

| Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | Resolution |
|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|------------|
| 14:1 | Blindness age | "fifty-eight years [old]" | "fifty-eight years old" | "fifty-eight years old" | All agree: **58** (Sinaiticus) — Vaticanus's 158 is noted below |
| 14:2 | Family gathering | "the six-sons of his-son" | "the six grandsons" | "his six grandchildren" | **LOGOS** — "grandsons" most precise; PNEUMA's "grandchildren" is fine but less specific |
| 14:3 | Prophet citation | "Nahum" | "Nahum" | "the prophet Nahum" | All agree: **Nahum** per Sinaiticus |
| 14:3 | Tobit's confidence | "I-trust all the-words" | "I believe all the words" | "I believe with all my heart" | **LOGOS** — PNEUMA adds "with all my heart" not in Greek; *pisteuo* = "believe/trust" either works |
| 14:5 | Temple term | "house of God" | "house of God" | "temple of God" | **LOGOS/EMET** — *oikos* = "house"; "temple" (PNEUMA) is interpretive |
| 14:6 | Temporal clause | "until the-time-when the-times-of the-age are-fulfilled" | "until the time when the appointed season is fulfilled" | "not until the appointed time" | **LOGOS** — "appointed season" best captures *ho kairos*; EMET's redundancy ("times...age") is literal but confusing |
| 14:7 | Idol deception | "who-lead-astray them erroneously" | "which have led them into error" | "that have been lying to them for generations" | **LOGOS** — "led into error" is most accurate; PNEUMA's "for generations" is not in source |
| 14:8 | Eschatological exclusion | "will-be-absent from all the-earth" | "will be absent from all the earth" | "will be gone from the earth entirely" | **LOGOS** — preserves the unusual verb *apoleleimenoi* (absent/left out); PNEUMA's "entirely" redundant |
| 14:9 | *Eleēmosyna* | transliterated | "give alms" | "give to those in need" | **LOGOS** — "alms/almsgiving" is the established English term |
| 14:10 | Nadan relationship | "his-brother's-[son]" | "his brother's son" | "his nephew" | **LOGOS** — more precise; "nephew" is ambiguous across cultures |
| 14:10 | Ahikar's salvation | "escaped the-death-trap" | "saved from the deadly snare" | "his generosity that saved him" | **LOGOS** — "deadly snare" (*pagis*) preserves the trap-image which is the point of the parable |
| 14:11 | Moral conclusion | formal parallel structure | "see what almsgiving does...it kills!" | "See what generosity does...it kills its owner" | **LOGOS** — "kills!" without "its owner" is closer to Greek; PNEUMA's addition weakens the rhetorical force |
| 14:14 | Tobias's aged honor | "he-grew-old honorably" | "He grew old with honor" | "He grew old with grace and dignity" | **LOGOS** — single term *meta timēs*; PNEUMA doubles |
| 14:15 | Witness to Nineveh | "he-saw and he-heard of the-destruction" | "He saw and heard of the destruction" | "He lived long enough to hear the news" | **LOGOS/EMET** — PNEUMA drops "saw" (*eiden*); the dual witness (seeing + hearing) is in the Greek and is rhetorically important as the fulfillment of prophecy |

---

## Critical Textual Notes

**Sinaiticus vs. Vaticanus age figures:**
- Sinaiticus (GII, base text): Tobit blind at 58, regains sight at 66, total lifespan implied ~112; Tobias dies at 99
- Vaticanus (GI): Tobit 158 years total; Tobias 127 years
- All agents follow Sinaiticus per project brief

**Nahum vs. Jonah (v. 3):**
The Sinaiticus text reads *Nahoum* (Nahum). Some Vetus Latina manuscripts and one Greek tradition read *Iona* (Jonah) — the more famous prophet against Nineveh. All agents correctly follow Sinaiticus. The choice of Nahum is likely more original: Nahum 1–3 predicts the total, violent destruction of Nineveh, which is exactly what Tobit predicts in vv. 3–5. Jonah's message was one of potential repentance; Nahum's is unconditional doom — more appropriate to the eschatological finality Tobit is pronouncing.

**Historical confusion (v. 15):**
Tobit says Nineveh was captured by "Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus." Historically, Nineveh fell in 612 BCE to Nabopolassar of Babylon and Cyaxares of Media — not Nebuchadnezzar (who was crown prince at the time but became famous later) and not Ahasuerus (a Persian title used for multiple kings). The author is either working from a different tradition, using familiar names typologically, or blending historical memories. All three agents render the names as given in the Greek without correction. This is a feature of the text to be noted, not emended.

**The Ahikar connection (v. 10):**
The Ahikar tale (*Story of Ahikar*) was widely circulated in Aramaic, Syriac, Greek, and other traditions — a popular wisdom narrative about a wise scribe betrayed by his adopted son Nadan, then vindicated. Tobit is presented in some versions of the Ahikar story as Ahikar's kinsman. The author of Tobit uses the Ahikar story as a moral mirror: just as Ahikar's generosity (*eleēmosyna*) saved him from the trap his wicked nephew set, so Tobit's whole life has been one of *eleēmosyna* that saved him. The book ends where it began — with the practice of righteous giving.

**Disagreement count: 14**

— SOPHIA
